video_title: Henrik Zeberg: Why Bonds May Be Too Cheap
gist: Macro strategist Henrik Zeberg (Swissblock, Zeberg Letter) tells Wealthion's Maggie Lake that the US is late-cycle, not early-cycle: the 12-month average of nonfarm payroll job creation is near a standstill and a 2-3% consumer savings rate means a supply-driven inflation impulse has no one to carry it, making stagflation a narrative rather than a state. He argues Treasuries are mispriced because they are too cheap, equities are set up for a 2000-style blow-off top that could take the Nasdaq to 37,000-39,000 before an Eiffel-Tower crash, and the dollar falls toward DXY 93-94 before a violent bust-driven squeeze higher.

themes.theme: Payroll data hides a labor standstill

insights.claim: The 12-month moving average of US nonfarm payroll job creation is running near 50,000 jobs per month, and the latest revision cut the April 2025-to-March 2026 period to roughly 16,000 jobs per month, which Zeberg calls a standstill.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: If the smoothed job-creation trend is already at recession-entry levels, growth-sensitive assets are priced off a labor picture the monthly headline is masking.
insights.quote: That means from April 25 to March 26, we had 16,000 jobs a month per month. That is a standstill.

insights.claim: Zeberg says the 12-month average of US job creation is now lower on a nominal basis than it was going into every recession of the past 50 to 60 years, and worse still when measured as a share of population.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable, chartable monthly test of whether the late-cycle thesis is holding.
insights.quote: it's lower than it's been going into all recessions 50, 60 years back

insights.claim: The 162,000-job headline print rested on a 44% establishment-survey response rate, the lowest on record, with the missing 56% assumed to have hired like the responders; if the non-responders hired half as fast the number falls toward 120,000 or below, and the BLS's own 90% confidence range spans 40,000 to 280,000 jobs.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: The imputation and noise band are wider than the market-moving surprise, so fade knee-jerk payroll reactions and wait for revisions.
insights.quote: It was 44%, which is the lowest we have seen in, you know, as far back we can go.

themes.theme: Inflation needs a consumer to carry it

insights.claim: Zeberg's core inflation framework is that a supply shock only becomes sustained inflation if someone can pass it on, so with no demand there is no inflation regardless of oil or commodity spikes.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Reframes oil and copper spikes as a tax on the consumer rather than a reason to price persistent inflation, favoring duration over inflation hedges near term.
insights.quote: Inflation is not something that comes down from the sky and you know punishes us. It's something that we carrying it carrying on ourselves.

insights.claim: The 1970s analogy fails because the US consumer savings rate is now 2-3% versus above 10% (and 10-20% at the extremes) in the 1970s, removing the buffer households then used to absorb higher prices and keep an inflationary cycle running.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable reason to discount 1970s-style stagflation positioning such as short duration and long commodities.
insights.quote: the consumer savings at this point is down to 2 to 3%

insights.claim: Zeberg rejects the stagflation label at current readings, defining real stagflation as roughly 6-7% inflation alongside 7-8% unemployment, and notes CPI near 3.5% is not high for this point in the business cycle given inflation was materially higher at the comparable stages of 2001 and 2007.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Suggests the stagflation trade is a crowded narrative rather than a regime, and is vulnerable to a growth-scare unwind.
insights.quote: stagflation is when you have inflation of 6, 7% something like that, and you have uh unemployment levels around 7, 8% or something like that. That that is real stagflation

insights.claim: Zeberg places the genuine stagflation risk after the downturn, when Fed stimulus meets a damaged real economy, citing the 2022 episode of nine months of simultaneous bond and equity declines as the template rather than the present moment.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Sequences the trade: own duration into the bust, then rotate into inflation hedges as stimulus arrives on the other side.
insights.quote: That's the that's the risk of the inflation not when the economy is slowing.

insights.claim: Zeberg names Treasuries as the clearest mispricing in markets right now because they are too cheap, directly against the consensus that rates must rise on sticky inflation.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: This is the episode's headline trade: long duration against a market positioned for hikes.
insights.quote: bonds you know, treasuries and so on looks very mispriced, but that's because they're too cheap at this point here

insights.claim: Zeberg argues the Fed's policy rate is at the wrong level because the central bank is honoring only its inflation mandate while job creation sits at standstill levels, and he attacks the 2% target as an arbitrary artifact traced to Greenspan in the 1990s and formalized around 2012, noting growth was historically best with inflation near 3 to 3.5%.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A dovish pivot driven by the employment mandate, or a challenge to the target itself, would reprice the short end and the long end structurally.
insights.quote: We got to kill the consumer in the pursuit of of of getting inflation down.

insights.claim: Central banks are repeating the 2008 error of tightening into weakness, with the ECB having hiked in June-July 2008 while its own outlook of above 3-3.5% inflation proved wrong and the eurozone fell into deflation.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for buying duration ahead of a forecast-driven policy mistake by the ECB and BOJ.
insights.quote: we saw the ECB doing that in 2008. It was a massive mistake.

insights.claim: In January 2008 the Fed cut sharply while inflation was at 4% and still rising, showing the central bank abandons the inflation mandate abruptly once labor and liquidity data break.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Precedent that cuts can arrive with inflation above target, so hawkish inflation prints are a poor guide to the next Fed move.
insights.quote: the Fed actually hiked by sorry cut by a 225 basis point in January of 2008 while inflation was at 4% and rising

insights.claim: Zeberg rejects the argument that the top 10% of asset owners now drive economic growth, arguing no K-shaped economy has ever been persistent and that GDP growth and job creation are highest when the middle class is strong.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the bull case that wealth-effect spending can sustain corporate earnings while the bottom 70% weakens.
insights.quote: If they can't afford bread, let them eat cake.

insights.claim: The median US consumer by income cannot absorb an unexpected $2,000 bill such as a car repair, more Americans live paycheck to paycheck than at any prior point including the peak of the financial crisis, and the US housing market remains frozen solid.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A thin household buffer plus frozen housing means any income shock transmits straight into discretionary spending and consumer-facing earnings.
insights.quote: the median consumer in the US looking at from income level will not be able to to handle a $2,000 uh extra bill

insights.claim: Zeberg frames AI adoption as a gearbox-shift loss of momentum, with workers over 50 in decent-paying jobs being made redundant now, and argues post-COVID rate cuts merely pulled durable-goods consumption forward from the future rather than creating new demand.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Links the AI capex boom to the very demand destruction that would undermine the earnings supporting AI valuations, with no easy stimulus fix for the durables air pocket.

themes.theme: Blow-off top then Eiffel Tower crash

insights.claim: Zeberg expects a final melt-up that could take the Nasdaq to 37,000-39,000 very quickly over roughly the next one to three months before the cycle turns, making the picture very different by New Year's.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A specific upside target and window for anyone trying to ride the last leg before de-risking into year-end.
insights.quote: I think we could see 37, 39,000 on the Nasdaq and uh and in in in a very very fast manner.

insights.claim: Zeberg's trigger for calling the top is short-term yields dropping really sharply, which he says is not happening yet and is precisely why he still allows for higher equity prices.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, monitorable signal to time the switch from melt-up participation to defense.
insights.quote: what I'm looking for this specifically will be that the short-term yield start to drop really sharply. And we don't see that.

insights.claim: The 2000 analogue Zeberg cites is a 45% Nasdaq rally in the final seven weeks into the top, followed by a near-40% drop in only two to three weeks, a pattern he says never resolves sideways and which he sees already playing out in silver's crash and the topping of South Korea's KOSPI.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Quantifies the asymmetry of chasing a blow-off top and points to cross-asset tells that speculative leadership is already breaking.
insights.quote: In 2000, we actually saw the last 7 weeks into the top stock market top. We saw a 45% rally in the Nasdaq. 45% in 7 weeks.

insights.claim: Zeberg dismisses the search for a catalyst, noting there was none on the day of the October 2007 top, and uses an avalanche model in which the underlying structure grows more unstable the longer the top persists, naming circular revenue recognition among AI businesses as one candidate trigger.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Argues against waiting for a news trigger to de-risk, and flags AI vendor-financing and circular revenue disclosure as the specific accounting risk to monitor.
insights.quote: I do know that the longer it persists, it's not like then it's becoming better and better. It's becoming more and more unstable.

insights.claim: Zeberg says copper is very close to a potential top, comparing today's copper bullishness to the 2008 China-will-buy-all-the-oil narrative that preceded oil's collapse from roughly $140-150 per barrel.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A near-term de-risking or short signal in industrial metals, and a warning that the demand narrative peaks with the price.
insights.quote: I think we're very close to a potential top in the uh at least in copper, I would say.

insights.claim: Zeberg separates oil from copper on the grounds that Hormuz and Iran geopolitics can sustain the oil spike longer, even though he expects the same eventual demand-driven break.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Suggests expressing the commodity-top view in copper first, since oil still carries an unresolved geopolitical premium.

insights.claim: Zeberg is bearish the dollar near term and sees the DXY falling to around 93-94 after trading above 100 only a month ago, driven by the market realizing the Fed is less hawkish than assumed.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A defined downside target that would mark the point to flip from short dollar to long dollar.
insights.quote: I think we can see the see the dollar dropping the Dixie down to around 93 94. We are already sometime some some way down there. We were above 100 just a month ago.

insights.claim: Zeberg is massively bullish the dollar into any bust, arguing a world effectively short the dollar must close credit lines and meet margin calls in dollars, producing a dollar shortage if the AI bubble bursts that eventually forces the Fed to intervene.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Frames long dollar as the crisis hedge and explains why dollar-debasement talk peaks precisely at this point in the cycle.
insights.quote: the dollar is the wrecking ball that can crush the rest of the world with the with its strength and it will be self-propelling

insights.claim: In the cash-shortage phase of a bursting bubble Zeberg expects gold hoarded by Asian and other countries to be sold off alongside good businesses that fall below fair value, so gold and Bitcoin do not work as safe havens at the moment of stress, though he is very bullish commodities, gold and silver in the phase after, once Fed backstops meet permanently higher consumer inflation expectations.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Challenges the standard crisis-hedge allocation: the entry point for hard assets is after the liquidation, not before it.

insights.claim: Zeberg frames the crypto rally as capital rotating out of extended Nasdaq and AI themes, noting crypto's roughly $1 trillion size against a global stock market near $150 trillion means small flows move it a lot.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: The relative-size argument explains why crypto can still make new highs even as he expects the broader cycle to roll over.
insights.quote: what comes into crypto is like 1 trillion out of a stock market of 150 trillion

insights.claim: Zeberg expects a new all-time high on Ethereum and on the altcoin index, but is not confident Bitcoin makes a new high, seeing a bounce toward 115,000 as more likely after what he reads as a bigger break.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A specific relative-value call favoring ETH and alts over BTC into the final euphoria leg.
insights.quote: I think we can see a new all-time high on Ethereum. Not so certain about Bitcoin like the rest of, you know, like everybody else's.

insights.claim: Zeberg's exit rule for crypto is the dollar bottoming, and he dismisses crypto as a future competitor to dollar hegemony, expecting it to be useful technology that supports AI rather than a rival to the DXY.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Ties the crypto exit to a single observable macro variable and separates tradable crypto beta from the debasement story used to justify holding forever.
insights.quote: When everybody's crying the dollar's dying, I probably will not be long crypto at that point. I'll probably sell it off.
